To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hFABF binds two molecules of oleic acid with an apparent Kd of 0.24 and 2.1 microM.

fatty acid binding to hFABP causes a sort of disagregation, which is reflected in the 1H-NM spectrum, that His is not involved in the interaction, that Lys is marginally involved, and that Arg is involved to a larger extent.

hFABPs bind two molecules of fatty acids in one binding site and that the fatty acid-binding site of the protein is located on the surface and is not shielded by the secondary structure of the protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of fatty acids with the neutral fatty-acid binding protein from bovine hepatic cytosol.
the interactions between fatty acid and hFABP and the conformational changes in hFABPs upon binding of fatty acid.
the elucidation of the structure-function relationship in fatty acid/protein binding.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the fatty acid/proteins interactions in hFABF are of a hydrophobic nature, and are mainly due to the binding of the hydrophobic part of the fatty acid, whereas electrostatic interactions do not play a significant role.
fatty acid/protein binding is a complex process which is influenced by several factors.

the binding of two molecules of oleic acid to hFABP is accompanied by conformational rearrangements of the protein, and that the binding is mainly governed by the electrostatic interactions of the fatty acid with the cationic amino acid groups on the surface of hFABPs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hFABPs are a family of proteins that bind fatty acids, and that their binding sites are not identical.
the binding of oleic to hFABP is a cooperative process, and that the protein undergoes structural alterations upon fatty acid binding.
the binding of fatty acid to hFABP induces a conformational change of the protein, which may be due to the disaggregation of the protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the binding of fatty acids to hFABP is a complex process, involving a number of different interactions, and that the binding site of hFABPs is probably different from that of other FABPs.

hFABPs are a heterogeneous class of proteins, and their fatty acid binding properties are different from those reported for FABP from the intestine and adipose tissue, as well as for the liver FABP of other species.
